content: Both studies were assessed to have a serious to very serious risk of bias according to the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). One study scored 3 out of 9 on the NOS, with downgrades due to the lack of control groups, failure to adjust for confounding variables, and absence of reporting on non-response rates. Using the Cochrane ROB-2 tool, some concerns regarding the risk of bias were identified. In terms of inconsistency, no serious issues were noted. However, indirectness was rated as serious and downgraded by one level due to the lack of information on the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) framework, specifically regarding the intervention of work exclusion for 21 days. Direct comparisons were unavailable. Imprecision was rated as very serious, with one study scoring 6 out of 9 on the NOS. This study was downgraded for the absence of a non-exposed cohort and failure to adjust for key confounders. It was further downgraded by two levels due to very few or no events being reported and the lack of relative effect estimates. Additionally, it was downgraded by one level due to the small sample size, which precluded the evaluation of relative effects. Data on infection with Ebola or Marburg viruses were derived from six studies. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to serious risk of bias, serious indirectness, and very serious imprecision. There is uncertainty regarding whether continuing normal duties (without work exclusion) increases or decreases the risk of infection with Ebola or Marburg viruses. Similarly, there is uncertainty about whether continuing normal duties affects healthcare-associated transmission of Ebola. A systematic review published in 2021 evaluated the efficacy of chlorine-based surface disinfection against seven pathogens, including Ebola virus. For completeness, the titles and abstracts of 89 laboratory studies included in the systematic review were reviewed, along with 25 more recent studies that cited the review. Four additional articles were deemed relevant and screened at the full-text stage, but none met the eligibility criteria. No studies provided data comparing the efficacy of wiping versus spraying for any disinfection agent in a controlled laboratory setting. Gallandat et al. (2021) conducted a systematic review of chlorine-based surface disinfection efficacy to inform recommendations for low-resource outbreak settings. Among the 89 studies reviewed, the most common modes of disinfectant application were pipetting (61%), immersion (22%), spraying (9%), and wiping (6%). Wiping was found to have an effect on viruses and spores even in the absence of disinfectant, suggesting that the mechanical action of wiping contributes to reducing contamination levels on surfaces. A study comparing wiping and spraying showed similar efficacy against Clostridioides difficile spores, but spraying was considered less appropriate for healthcare settings due to extended drying times and its inability to remove dirt and debris. Ensuring contact between the disinfectant and test organisms was noted as a challenge with spraying. Additionally, chlorine loss during spraying, from the nozzle to the targeted surface, was identified as a concern. Lantagne et al. (2018) conducted an experimental study to test the efficacy of disinfectants in preventing the transmission of emerging infectious diseases. The study evaluated the impacts of chlorine chemistry, the efficacy of surface cleaning recommendations, and the safety and efficacy of handwashing recommendations. A testing matrix was developed, including various surface types (nitrile, heavy-duty tarp, stainless steel), chlorine types (NaDCC, HTH, generated NaOCl, stabilized NaOCl), soil load (with and without), and factors varying between recommendations from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), WHO, and CDC. The bacteriophage most similar to the Ebola virus was dried on an 8 cm diameter disc for one hour, and disinfection was carried out with or without pre-treatment. Residual contamination was measured at the end of the exposure time. The study found that 0.5% chlorine solutions with a 15-minute exposure time were effective in reducing transmission risk. Pre-cleaning practices such as wiping or covering did not increase disinfection efficacy, though covering could limit splashing. Gallandat et al. (2017) compared the efficacy of four chlorine solutions (sodium hypochlorite, sodium dichloroisocyanurate, high-test hypochlorite, and generated hypochlorite) for disinfecting three surface types (stainless steel, heavy-duty tarp, and nitrile) with and without pre-cleaning practices (pre-wiping, covering, or both) and soil load. The test organisms were Escherichia coli and the Ebola surrogate Phi6. The study concluded that 0.5% chlorine, regardless of chlorine type, surface, pre-cleaning practices, or organic matter, was effective in interrupting disease transmission from uncontrolled spills during Ebola outbreaks. No studies were found that provided data on adverse effects associated with chemical exposure, coverage of surfaces with disinfectant, or log reduction of viruses or surrogates on surfaces. Similarly, no studies met the eligibility criteria for evaluating infection with Ebola or Marburg viruses, psychological effects (e.g., stigma) associated with spraying homes with disinfectants, or staff exposure during the handling and laundering of linens. Edmunds et al. (2016) identified waste products from the care of individuals with Ebola virus disease and developed flow diagrams to show the creation of such products. They identified 13 critical control points where measures could be adopted to reduce transmission risks. Garibaldi et al. (2017) validated autoclave protocols for decontaminating category A medical waste. The study found that saturated linens required a vacuum cycle of at least 60 minutes to achieve adequate sterilization. Shorter sterilization times failed in all cases. Haverkort et al. (2016) reported that waste management was a major concern in preparing to admit Ebola patients, with waste destruction outsourced due to insufficient in-hospital autoclave capacity. Otter et al. (2010) described the use of hydrogen peroxide vapor for decontaminating a critical care unit room contaminated with blood and body fluids from a patient with Lassa fever.
